stories.summary: Citing a statistic he got from Karthik Muralidharan, Amit describes a government advertisement for 368 peon posts that drew about two and a half million applicants, roughly 250 of them PhDs. That works out to around 6,500 applicants per job (his figures, 'something to that effect'). He sets this beside entrepreneur friends who say they can't find skilled people, which is why job-hopping is rampant in Bangalore.
stories.insight: Mass unemployment and a skills shortage exist side by side because degrees are being handed out without the abilities they claim to certify. The gap isn't only vocational. Many graduates can't really read, understand text, or make sense of the world.
stories.quote: Three hundred and sixty eight peon jobs, two and a half million people applied for it, including two hundred and fifty PhDs.

stories.summary: After moving to Bombay in the 1990s, Amit commuted by local train. He found it heartbreaking that first-class passengers were, on average, significantly taller than those in second class. A lifetime of different nutrition had written social class onto people's bodies.
stories.insight: Deprivation in childhood leaves marks. Stunted height is visible. The stunting that bad education does to minds is just as real but unseen, so we rarely reckon with it.
stories.quote: it was heartbreaking to see that the people in first class were on average significantly taller than the people in second class. That is visible, that is a seen. What is unseen is what the lack of education also does to people.

stories.summary: India's education bureaucracy long resisted the OECD's PISA test. Under international pressure it allowed a limited round, and it handpicked Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu in the hope of looking good. Their 15-year-olds instead ranked among the worst in the world. Ajay recalls that the bureaucracy then ran away from the project and stopped measuring, and he isn't sure much of the micro data was ever released.
stories.insight: A state that controls money and power but avoids accountability would rather not know than measure. The cover-up tells you what the system is really optimising for.
stories.quote: the Indian bureaucracy chose Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu hoping that it would make India look good. And it didn't.

stories.topic: The Upper-Tail Bump: India's Hidden Talent Pool
stories.summary: India's PISA score distribution has a small bump at the top, meaning an unusual number of 15-year-olds with remarkably high scores. Someone took that percentage and multiplied it by India's cohort of 15-year-olds. Ajay can't recall whether it was him or Lant Pritchett. The answer was that India has perhaps the second- or third-largest plausible scientific and engineering workforce in the world.
stories.insight: India tells two stories at once: a tiny core at the top that is outrageously good, and a mainline that is horrible. Pointing to the IITs says nothing about the typical child.
stories.quote: lo and behold, you get an answer that India is the second largest or the third largest plausible scientific and engineering workforce in the world.

stories.topic: When Even an IAS Family Couldn't Afford to Fly
stories.summary: Amit, son of an IAS officer, can't recall taking a domestic flight as a child in the 1980s. It was too expensive even for his family, who flew only on a foreign holiday every three years or so. Getting a telephone line took five or six years. After the 1991 reforms let markets into airlines and telecom, both became cheap and widely accessible, and state operators like MTNL and BSNL became essentially irrelevant.
stories.insight: Where India allowed markets, access exploded. In education, which matters most, it didn't. Amit's plea is not to privatise everything, only to stop constraining private players and see what happens.
stories.quote: I was a son of an IAS officer. I really can't recall travelling by a domestic flight. It was too much even for us, right?

stories.topic: Karthik vs Lant: Does Education Cause Development?
stories.summary: Amit once assumed that a country educates its people first and develops afterwards. When first told otherwise he resisted, until the data changed his mind more than a decade ago. On his show, Karthik Muralidharan had implied that development follows education. Lant Pritchett, in a later episode, said there is no evidence for that and that causality runs the other way. After the Lant episode, Amit's friend Murali Neelakantan tweeted that it might be a two-way virtuous cycle. Amit says the cold hard data backs Lant.
stories.insight: Smart experts genuinely disagree on whether schooling drives growth. Amit's own reversal shows a deeply held, intuitive belief giving way to evidence.
stories.quote: Murali was musing aloud that maybe it's like a two way relationship and it's a virtuous cycle. And actually it's not.

stories.summary: Nehru's generation saw Britain, with near-universal schooling and Oxford and Cambridge, as the model. At independence India's female literacy was about 6%. Ajay imagines bringing Nehru to 2024 and telling him literacy is now around 75%. Nehru would assume India must be at 60–70% of UK per capita GDP. We would have to hang our heads and admit India is a lower-middle-income country at about a tenth of the global frontier.
stories.insight: India ran the 'educate first, prosperity follows' experiment for decades. The literacy arrived and the prosperity didn't, which is a homegrown version of Pritchett's finding.
stories.quote: if you went back to Jawaharlal Nehru in a time machine and said, you know, 2024 we got like seventy-five percent literacy in India. And he'd say, oh great, wow.

stories.summary: Ajay recalls an interview in which James Heckman, he thinks only half kidding, said the world has two problems. Graduate students are starving for money, and children in disadvantaged families lack exposure to ideas. Pay the grad students to sit with the kids and talk to them about ideas and the world, and you solve both.
stories.insight: Much of a child's cognitive development comes from hearing rich, complex adult conversation. That is cheap to provide and enormously valuable, yet affluent homes now drown it out with mass media and test prep.
stories.quote: there are two problems in the world. There is a problem of starving graduate students, starving PhD students... and there is a problem of children in disadvantaged families. And the great solution of the world is to bring both together.

stories.topic: Josh Felman's Theory of Jewish Achievement
stories.summary: Ajay asked Josh Felman why Jews have such outsized intellectual achievements, including the most Nobel laureates per capita. The standard answer is selection. Repeated pogroms meant people with portable human capital fled and flourished, while those holding land and physical businesses didn't. Felman offered another answer. In the religious gathering, held at home rather than in a formal institution, it isn't a priest who speaks. Each person takes a turn delivering a 10–15 minute oration that weaves the religious text into their own life.
stories.insight: When a culture makes every ordinary member regularly synthesise ideas and say them out loud, it builds intellectual capability at scale. Book clubs and learning circles can recreate this.
stories.quote: Every single person who went through that religious tradition was pushing on this ability of combining a religious book with everyday life and experiences and articulating it as a 10-20 minute oration.

stories.summary: Amit recalls that he and Ajay first had meaningful interactions at a book club run by a friend. Ajay's story reminds him of a weekly Thursday ritual at the Takshashila Institution in Bangalore. One by one, researchers such as Nitin Pai plug their laptops into the projector and present what they learned that week, often outside their own field.
stories.insight: Rituals of sharing what you learned turn learning into something social and multidisciplinary. 'Everything is everything' becomes an institutional habit.
stories.quote: one by one they will connect their laptop to the projector and they'll give a brief presentation on what they learned that week.

stories.topic: The IIT Director and the JEE
stories.summary: Ajay asked a wise, good director of IIT Tirupati how the JEE's role in IIT admissions could be reduced. The director said it would be a nightmare, hard to do, and would bring litigation. Ajay pointed out that the IIMs had already done it by adding interviews and group discussions and reducing the weight of the exam.
stories.insight: Reforms that look impossible from inside often have a working precedent next door. The real obstacle is a centralised mindset, not feasibility.
stories.quote: I said, look, the IIMs have done it. The IIMs have prized open and reduced the emphasis on the examination.

stories.topic: Why a Former Cricket Writer Skips the IPL
stories.summary: Amit was a cricket journalist for years and followed the game deeply. He has stopped following it completely. Asked why he doesn't watch the IPL, he said it would eat his evenings for a month and a half.
stories.insight: Deep learning needs protected time. Every shallow distraction has an opportunity cost, so Amit advises young people to immerse in subjects instead of flitting between them.
stories.quote: Somebody asked me why aren't you following the IPL? I have said that for you know then for one and a half months my evenings are gone. I cannot do that. The opportunity cost is too high.

recommendations.item: The Collected Stories of Lydia Davis
recommendations.creator: Lydia Davis
recommendations.context: Amit's end-of-episode pick, which he calls both unrelated and related to education.
recommendations.reason: Fiction lets you enter the minds of others and live their lives. Davis is 'one of the great modern writers', and many of her stories are a paragraph or less. Literature keeps you learning without feeling like you are in learning mode.

recommendations.item: Essays
recommendations.creator: Lydia Davis
recommendations.context: Recommended as a companion to her collected stories.
recommendations.reason: Davis writing about her own craft and literature, 'and much more besides'.

recommendations.item: To Kill a Mockingbird
recommendations.creator: Harper Lee
recommendations.context: Ajay's pick, following Amit's lead in recommending literature.
recommendations.reason: Growing up, he read it as a masterpiece about the minds of a parent and a child facing bigotry he assumed was in the past. Now he finds it a hundred times more relevant, because history never ended and that darkness is still around us.

recommendations.item: The Beautiful Tree
recommendations.creator: James Tooley
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the chapter on private enterprise in education.
recommendations.reason: A 'wonderful book' on budget private schools serving the poor, grounded in work among poor families and how they actually choose. 'Do read that as well.'

recommendations.item: Private Education Is Good for the Poor
recommendations.creator: James Tooley and Pauline Dixon
recommendations.context: Cited to challenge the idea that private schools are only for the rich.
recommendations.reason: Their Hyderabad study found many slum dwellers chose to pay for budget private schools over free government ones.

recommendations.item: How Much Does Free Education Cost?
recommendations.creator: Centre for Civil Society
recommendations.context: Cited alongside the Tooley–Dixon study.
recommendations.reason: A Delhi survey of households earning under Rs 5,000 a month found the same thing: a large share send their kids to budget private schools.

recommendations.item: The Aser Reports
recommendations.creator: Aser Centre
recommendations.context: Amit draws his headline learning-outcome numbers from Aser and says he'll link the site so listeners can go through the older reports too.
recommendations.reason: Simple measurement of learning done at scale every year. Ajay calls it the glory of the field and a milestone in Indian education.

recommendations.item: Accelerating India's Development
recommendations.creator: Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Amit describes it as a recent book on the Indian state with a good chapter on education.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of findings that more spending on buildings and toilets, on hiring 'better' teachers, or on inputs like school bags and midday meals does nothing for learning outcomes.

recommendations.item: Where Has All the Education Gone?
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Ajay introduces this 2001 paper in the chapter on education and development. Amit later urges listeners to read it in full and follow its citations.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it one of the most important papers in the history of development economics. It is a cold cross-country statistical analysis finding that expanding schooling produced essentially zero growth.

recommendations.item: The first PISA results for India: The end of the beginning
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Linked with Ajay's account of India's limited PISA round in Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
recommendations.reason: Pritchett on what India's first PISA results revealed.

recommendations.item: PISA
recommendations.creator: OECD
recommendations.context: Ajay presents it as one of the two numbers anyone in the field must know.
recommendations.reason: It tests a household-based random sample of 15-year-olds, not just those in school, on applying science and maths rather than rote memory. You need a rough sense of its scores to take part in any serious education debate.

recommendations.item: James Heckman's work on early childhood / The Heckman Equation
recommendations.creator: James Heckman
recommendations.context: Ajay introduces Heckman's research in the early-childhood chapter. Amit says it shook him when he first heard of it.
recommendations.reason: Hard-nosed return-on-investment evidence that the biggest payoffs come from interventions at ages 0–3 or 0–5, especially for disadvantaged children. That includes cognitive basics, social-emotional learning, and what kids overhear.

recommendations.item: Google Scholar's citations list
recommendations.context: A trick Amit says he learned from Ajay the day before recording.
recommendations.reason: Open any paper, click its citation count, and you see every later paper that engaged with it, both critics and follow-ups. It's a way to go down real rabbit holes.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Half in jest, Ajay proposes it to Heckman as an experiment for children aged 0–5 and 5–17.
recommendations.reason: He suggests every parent consider it 'a soundtrack of the child's life'. The serious point is that children gain a lot from overhearing rich adult conversations about ideas.

recommendations.item: Natasha Badhwar Lives the Examined Life (Episode 301, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Recommended to every parent in the chapter on what parents should do.
recommendations.reason: Badhwar is an incredible person and writer on parenting who homeschools her kids. The episode has a lot of thinking on how to educate your children.

recommendations.item: The Takshashila Institution
recommendations.context: Mentioned while discussing learning communities.
recommendations.reason: Its weekly ritual of researchers presenting what they learned that week is Amit's living example of multidisciplinary group learning. He says it leaves your brain cells all fired up.

recommendations.item: Fixing Indian Education (Episode 185, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: One of the many Seen and the Unseen episodes on education that Amit links.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation with Karthik Muralidharan, whose research on spending and incentives underpins much of this episode's diagnosis.

recommendations.item: Karthik Muralidharan and the Bureaucrat's Burden (Episode 375, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked alongside the Lant Pritchett episode in the education-and-development debate.
recommendations.reason: Gives Muralidharan's side of the debate, in which focusing on education was implied to be the route to development.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The episode that prompted Murali Neelakantan's tweets on education and development.
recommendations.reason: Lant argues that education and development are largely unlinked and that causality runs from development to education. Amit says the hard data backs this view.

recommendations.item: Education in India (Episode 77, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: One of the many education episodes Amit says he has done and links in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: An earlier long-form conversation with Amit Chandra on the state of Indian education.

recommendations.item: We Are Brains, Not Stomachs (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit invokes its idea while discussing India's potential.
recommendations.reason: A growing population is good because people are brains, not stomachs. That only pays off if those brains are trained to think, and India isn't doing that.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay links it when explaining why Aser mattered so much.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the policy pipeline, where change starts with information and research. That is where Ajay thinks philanthropy should put its money.

recommendations.item: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Episode 46, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit refers to the reaction it drew while urging young people to engage in good faith.
recommendations.reason: Many critics didn't engage with its arguments. They took a challenge to beliefs like socialism as an attack on their identity, which Amit warns listeners not to do.

recommendations.item: Why India Needs School Vouchers
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Wall Street Journal piece from around 2007.
recommendations.reason: His early case for school vouchers, the episode's main proposal for spending public money better.

recommendations.item: Fund Schooling, Not Schools
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: A 2007 column whose title names this episode's third chapter.
recommendations.reason: The core voucher idea: public money should follow the child to whatever school the parent chooses.

recommendations.item: Our Unlucky Children
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: A 2007 piece from the twenty years Amit has spent writing about Indian education.
recommendations.reason: It shows how long the crisis has been visible. Amit says the problem is much older than his writing on it.

recommendations.item: It is immoral to have children. Here's why
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Mentioned while arguing that too many people jump into parenthood unprepared.
recommendations.reason: A provocative column, which Amit says is not the standard antinatalist argument. It backs his point that having children is a huge responsibility that goes beyond material comfort and a school seat.

recommendations.item: Geniuses and economic development
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked alongside the discussion of the top tail of India's PISA scores.
recommendations.reason: Ties to the idea that India's small but, in absolute numbers, huge pool of very capable people matters for development.

recommendations.item: Doing better than a competitive exam
recommendations.creator: Nitin Pai and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked to Ajay's advice that policy people be far more skeptical of competitive exams.
recommendations.reason: Ajay thinks UPSC, IIT-JEE and the 12th-standard boards are a bad way to organise education and wants their role reduced.

recommendations.item: Three page notes considered harmful
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked to Ajay's critique of the Indian state's bias for action.
recommendations.reason: It describes the pathology: a half-baked idea, a three-page note, three practitioners consulted, no thinkers at the table, and then a bad idea gets implemented.

core_ideas.explanation: The near-universal consensus says more money, teachers and schools. Yet Aser shows 57% of class five children can't read a class two text, and among 14–18-year-olds one in four can't read a class two text and half can't do class-three division. Karthik Muralidharan's findings show that spending on buildings, on hiring 'better' teachers, or on student inputs doesn't move outcomes. The real problem is design and incentives: a teacher works hard until made permanent, then stops showing up.
core_ideas.quote: I'd say the key thing is that it's not about more, it's about better.

core_ideas.concept: Data First: Juxtapose Spend (PPE) Against Outcomes (Aser/PISA)
core_ideas.explanation: Every debate on education spending should put two numbers side by side. One is per pupil expense: government education spending divided by the number of children actually in government schools. The other is an outcome measure like Aser or PISA. PPE has doubled and quadrupled while outcomes have stagnated or fallen. Measurement is where change starts; without it you thrash around for decades.
core_ideas.quote: the first step of the journey of change, of the road to change, is data.

core_ideas.concept: Most of India Is Sub-Saharan Africa
core_ideas.explanation: Elites look around their cafés and see startups and potential. Amit's point is that most Indians live in conditions comparable to sub-Saharan Africa. The people the elite think of as service staff are the actual middle class, and only a tiny sliver sits above them. Add a broken education system and the country's potential is being wasted on a huge scale.
core_ideas.quote: The people we think of as our chauffeurs and domestic help are actually the real middle class of India

core_ideas.explanation: Nehru-era hostility to profit led to rules banning for-profit schools, piles of licences (Amit recalls something like 42 to open a school in Delhi), and utopian regulations on playground size and toilet ratios. These choke supply. In competitive markets profit comes from serving people well. Airlines and telecom were opened up after 1991 and access boomed; education never was.
core_ideas.quote: in a competitive marketplace you earn a profit by serving something, in this case, serving better education.

core_ideas.explanation: Poor parents choose to pay perhaps Rs 4,000 a year for a budget private school over a free government school that spends around Rs 10,000 per pupil. Studies suggest private schools get similar or slightly better outcomes at about a third of the cost, and parents can hold them accountable. Parents also weigh things researchers miss, such as how safely a child can get to school.
core_ideas.quote: it is hair raising that they're choosing to go spend their own money.

core_ideas.explanation: An idea first proposed by Milton Friedman. Keep public spending, but give the per-child amount to parents as a voucher they can cash at any school, government or private. Schools then have to compete for students, and absentee teachers face consequences. Amit says not to let the perfect be the enemy of the good: if the money will be spent anyway, let parents direct it.
core_ideas.quote: I would say that the funding from the government can continue, but don't send it to the schools, give it to the parents.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay takes a milder but sharper position: leave government schools as they are, but stop abandoning children who leave them. Today the state spends on a child only if they stay in the government system. Fairness, and the Article 14 idea of equality, demands equal spending per child in India, not per child enrolled in public schools.
core_ideas.quote: Public spending should be symmetric per child.

core_ideas.explanation: Parents pushed for English-medium education even when government schools insisted on vernacular first languages. They understood that English is the link language and the ticket to progress. Educationists note the switch to an English-speaking household takes about three generations and hurts learning along the way. Ajay still sees private schools as the exit valve that let families start that journey.
core_ideas.quote: So the most powerful network of India is English.

core_ideas.explanation: Across countries and decades, more schooling produced essentially no growth. Haiti today has France's 1970 education numbers but none of its prosperity. Ajay offers three rival explanations. First, implementation failed, which fits India but not the global data. Second, education is mostly signalling, a Louis Vuitton bag that sorts people rather than teaching them. Third, we've defined education wrongly. The truth may be some of each. Counting learning outcomes instead of inputs explains part of the paradox, but not all of it.
core_ideas.quote: The answer was essentially zero. That there was no gain.

core_ideas.concept: The Industrial School Rewards Only Conscientiousness
core_ideas.explanation: Age-sorted classrooms, fixed curricula and rote procedures are a 19th-century design meant to produce factory workers and babus. Of the five big personality traits, this system measures and nurtures only conscientiousness, so obedient children thrive. What actually matters is flexible general intelligence: being able to look at rain falling on a roof and apply quadratic equations to a real question. In Ajay's words, education should kindle a fire, not fill a pail.
core_ideas.quote: So the kids that take orders, the kids who will obey are the ones who will flourish in the industrialized education system.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues the defining skill of the next twenty or thirty years is learning how to learn, which means thinking independently. His schooling taught him nothing; life taught him numeracy, probabilistic thinking and clear writing. He and Ajay are considering a 'Life Lessons' course to teach such things to people of any age.
core_ideas.quote: The key skill in modern times is learning how to learn.

core_ideas.concept: The Heckman Window and the Power of Overhearing
core_ideas.explanation: James Heckman's return-on-investment research points to early childhood, ages 0–3 or 0–5, especially for disadvantaged children, as the best place to intervene. The basics of reading and arithmetic matter, and so do social-emotional learning and regulating behaviour. Talking with a child and making eye contact matters, but a lot of learning comes from overhearing adults discuss ideas with a rich vocabulary. Amit adds that what is missed in those years can't be made up later.
core_ideas.quote: from age zero to three the child is adding one million neural connections per second.

core_ideas.concept: The Family Is Where Education Really Happens
core_ideas.explanation: Denmark has a rich welfare state and the US a thin one, yet family background predicts outcomes equally strongly in both. Knowledge moves through families almost without anyone noticing, through conversations, books that actually get discussed, and informal apprenticeships. Amit calls this an extra layer of privilege beyond money. Populist sneering at 'nepo babies' misses this, and schools can't replace it. Heckman's interventions therefore aim to improve the home itself.
core_ideas.quote: The family is a site where tremendous intergenerational transformation and knowledge flows take place.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues there's little a 10-year-old can teach another 10-year-old. In hunter-gatherer bands, children of mixed ages roamed as a pack, played, and gradually joined the real work. Adults benefit the same way. Ajay, at 58, counts a 25-year-old among the most important people in his life. Groups of the same age share one view of the world, which limits everyone in them.
core_ideas.quote: If you're a twenty-four year old surrounded by twenty-four year olds, you're doing something wrong.

core_ideas.concept: School Is Daycare: Don't Confuse It With Education
core_ideas.explanation: Amit warns parents not to treat school as daycare and consider their job done. Ajay goes further and says parents would be better off seeing that school really is just daycare. Real knowledge-building happens elsewhere: at home, through books, conversation and attention, and without piling on pressure.
core_ideas.quote: I think it would be a darn good thing if parents understood that school is a daycare, that college is daycare for teenagers, and no more. So do not confuse school with your education.

core_ideas.concept: The Integrated Mind vs the Technician
core_ideas.explanation: Some people are engineers at work and medieval in the rest of their lives, or they design chips all day and then watch Netflix. Ajay calls that a hole in the heart. A full person reads about everything and brings general intelligence to every part of life, from making dahi to starting a business to relationships.
core_ideas.quote: There are people who have compartmentalized their knowledge that there is a part of my brain in which I'm an electrical engineer. For the rest I live in the medieval age.

core_ideas.concept: The Ladder of Changing Your Mind
core_ideas.explanation: At the bottom are people who never change their minds. The attainable minimum is to dig in during the argument but shift your views 5–10% after a week of reflection, which Ajay calls gold. Higher up is thanking the person who changed your mind. Higher still is saying 'you're right' in the moment, and the greatest statement of all is 'I was wrong.' Surround yourself with smart people and serious book clubs where everyone has actually read the chapter.
core_ideas.quote: you should shift your priors by ten percent in reflection of high quality arguments from the other side.

core_ideas.explanation: The first victim is yourself: 'I'm from IIT, so I've arrived.' The second is how you judge others, dismissing people without degrees, as lazy HR departments do. Amit adds a nuance. Signalling and networks are real, so take the IIT track if it's rational. Just don't be single-track. Go deep into subjects instead of flirting with them.
core_ideas.quote: The greatest victims of credentialism are the credentialed ones.

core_ideas.explanation: Policy people should be far more skeptical of education spending and of competitive exams like UPSC, JEE and the boards. They should also resist central control from New Delhi, which makes every IIT and IIM the same, much like public sector banks. Each institution should have local autonomy and its own vision. Educators, too, should doubt their paradigm and stop measuring themselves by how many students cleared the IIT JEE.
core_ideas.quote: We need a thousand flowers to bloom

core_ideas.concept: Philanthropy Belongs at the Start of the Policy Pipeline
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says funding Aser was the most effective use of philanthropic capital ever, because data and research change how thinking people see a problem. A poor use of money is putting an ERP system on a broken government paradigm or lending staff to a joint secretary for small incremental fixes. Philanthropies also suffer a principal-agent problem: staff want visible wins they can claim credit for.
core_ideas.quote: the world's most effective use of philanthropic capital ever was the funding that went to Aser.

core_ideas.concept: Bias for Action: Good for Individuals, Bad for States
core_ideas.explanation: For a creator, acting first is how you learn. Amit admits the show's first episodes weren't great, but episode 50 beats episode one and episode 250 will beat episode 50. The state, though, wields coercive power over millions, so Ajay wants it slow, careful and doing less. Act in haste, repent at leisure.
core_ideas.quote: So if you're seeing like an individual who wants to learn bias for action is good, if you're seeing like a state, bias for action is not good.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Right after Ajay explains the 'upper tail bump' in India's PISA distribution, Amit says: 'You're looking very hot today. Can I give you an upper tail bump?'
Ajay introducing per pupil expense: 'The second number I would like to introduce for this field is called PPE. And no, that does not mean personal protective equipment.'
Ajay's 'orthodox ex-Ministry of Finance' view of education spending: 'the counterfactual that I would always ask is we would have done better by taking all that money and paying down debt.'

Ajay's plan for government schools: turn them into canteens. Kids study at private schools, a bell rings at noon, they run to the government school for the midday meal, and at 12:45 another bell sends them running back. 'So this is a great harmonious coexistence.'
Amit recalling the joke from the era of long waiting lists: 'when your daughter is born you book a scooter so that for her marriage it'll be ready.'
Ajay on education as pure signalling: it's a Louis Vuitton bag, or 'the up and coming North Indian business person who buys a used Mercedes to try to signal that she is so successful.'
Ajay on age-segregated schooling: being 'herded into a factory where you are a ten year old with other dumb ten year olds just like yourself.'

As rain falls during the outdoor shoot, Amit says 'the skies are crying at the state of the world.' After Ajay describes middle-class homes 'drenched in mass culture,' Amit adds: 'Right now we are getting drenched, but we will continue this episode.'
Ajay: 'it's easy to get a book accepted at a publisher, it's easy to sell 10,000 copies of a book. It is truly hard to get people to actually read a book.'

Ajay imitating a credential snob: 'Oh, this Amit guy, he doesn't particularly have any degrees. He doesn't have that Louis Vuitton bag. So he must be a clueless bugger.' Amit later: 'this man here went to IIT, this man here went abroad and got fancy PhD. This man here has no credentials whatsoever. We can still be friends, right?'
Ajay on philanthropists tinkering with a broken system: 'putting lipstick on a pig, of putting an ERP system on top of a broken government policy paradigm.'
Nehru's famous line to JRD Tata, 'do not speak to me of profit. It is a dirty word', cited by Amit as the root of the ban on for-profit education.
Lant Pritchett as 'the child saying that the emperor has no clothes' about the post-war global schooling enterprise. He likes to note that Haiti's education measures today match France's in 1970.
PISA's top performers: Finland has the world's highest scores, South Korea and Japan do very well, and limited testing in Shanghai showed astonishing results.

Amit on one-size-fits-all schooling: 'If you're going to test a monkey on how to climb a tree, you're also testing a fish on how to climb a tree.' He contrasts it with supermarkets offering forty types of ketchup and thirty types of ghee.
Ajay on what education should be: 'kindling the fire and not filling the pail.'
Ajay attributes 'do not confuse school with your education' to an old Unix fortune.
Nandan Nilekani's secret, as Ajay recounts it: switch off the cricket, Bollywood and politics that fill people's lives, and spend the freed bandwidth on books and the life of the mind.
Milton Friedman credited as the originator of school vouchers.
